Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Early years education Parents of baby girl killed at nursery fear unsafe sleeping ‘rife’ in sector across England Katie and John Meehan say responses to campaign they launched after death of daughter Genevieve must be ‘wake-up call’ Josh Halliday North of England editor Sun 9 Aug 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 09.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The parents of a nine-month-old girl who died after being placed in an unsafe sleeping position at nursery said they feared poor practice may be “rife” across England. Genevieve Meehan suffocated when she was strapped face down to a beanbag for an hour and 37 minutes at a nursery in Cheadle Hulme, Stockport, in May 2022. Kate Roughley, the nursery’s deputy manager, was jailed for 14 years in 2024 after being found guilty of manslaughter. One of Roughley’s colleagues was later jailed for the “deplorable” treatment of other babies in her care. Genevieve’s parents, Katie and John Meehan, have led a campaign with the charity the Lullaby Trust to strengthen safety and regulation of nurseries after a series of high-profile abuses. The sector has come under intense scrutiny in recent months after the cases of Vincent Chan and Nathan Bennett , nursery workers who sexually assaulted children in their care. View image in fullscreen Genevieve Meehan, who died in May 2022 at nine months old. Photograph: Greater Manchester Police/PA Chan was jailed in February for 18 years for molesting young children in a campaign of sexual abuse that was described as “every parent’s worst nightmare”, while Bennett was jailed in March for 24 years for raping and abusing young children in his care. Another nursery worker, Kimberley Cookson, was jailed in April over the death of 14-month-old Noah Sibanda, who had been physically restrained face-down with a blanket over his head while being put to sleep. As a result of Genevieve’s parents’ campaign , childcare settings in England will be banned from September from putting babies under 12 months to sleep in anything other than a cot. Ofsted, the regulator, will triple the number of unannounced inspections – adding an extra 3,000 visits a year, boosted by an additional £8m from the government – and inspect nurseries every four years instead of six. Each visit will scrutinise sleeping policies. Katie Meehan, 42, said she was “really shocked” by the extent of unsafe sleeping practice that had been revealed when nurseries wrote privately to the government about the planned changes this year. Some reported leaving babies to sleep in pushchairs “due to space limitations”, according to details shared with the Department for Education (DfE). Others put infants to sleep outside, adopting “forest school models or Scandinavian practices”. By law, nurseries are required to follow NHS safer sleep guidance – which includes laying the baby on their back in a cot or Moses basket – however, in the rules from September, the government will state: “Babies aged one year and under must only be placed to sleep in a cot.” Katie Meehan, who is working closely with the government and Ofsted, said the responses suggested unsafe sleeping may be “rife” across England and that they were a “wake-up call” for the regulator and officials. Some nursery owners said they would be forced to reduce the number of infants they take as a result of the new rules. Several raised concerns that this will ban smaller beds, such as dream coracles, which take up less space than a cot and have been widely adopted in recent years. John Meehan, 40, said he was concerned some nursery owners – many of whom are backed by private equity firms – were potentially putting profit before safety. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion “There are lots and lots of people out there who just want to do their absolute best and they go into that industry because they want to look after children,” he said. “But my impression from some of the responses is that they are taking too many children and there is a money incentive for them to do so, and that is a real concern.” Ministers are now considering whether to introduce mandatory CCTV to all nurseries in England , one of the key aims of the campaign. Olivia Bailey, the former early years minister who spearheaded the latest reforms, is understood to have been very persuaded by the arguments for mandatory CCTV. Katie Meehan said she was disappointed that Bailey lost her role in the reshuffle when Andy Burnham became prime minister. However, she is hopeful Burnham will take up the reforms, having met Genevieve’s family this year when he was mayor of Greater Manchester. She said Burnham was particularly supportive of their call for mandatory CCTV – which was crucial in securing Genevieve’s killer’s conviction – and that he had told them: “Genevieve was a child of Manchester and she was failed. We’ve got to make sure it doesn’t happen again.” The DfE said: “What happened to Genevieve was a tragedy, and her parents’ campaigning has already changed practice across the country. We will keep going until no family goes through what theirs has. Nurseries, vets and shops: the sectors where private equity plays a big role Read more “The vast majority of settings do a brilliant job, and the response to our updated guidance showed a sector that wants to get this right. But settings have long been legally required to follow NHS safer sleep guidance, and that is why we are working with the Lullaby Trust to make those expectations unambiguous, so there can be no excuses for unsafe practice.” Sir Martyn Oliver, the chief inspector at Ofsted, said: “No parent should have to endure what Katie and John have been through. They have shown remarkable bravery in pursuing change following their daughter’s tragic death. “We welcome the DfE’s additional funding for more frequent inspections, including thousands more without notice visits. We’re also strengthening our inspection practice so that safe sleeping in nurseries and with childminders is now a mandatory part of every inspection and will be reported on for parents to read.” Explore more on these topics Early years education Crime Ofsted Childcare Children Parents and parenting Child protection news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Education Schools Teachers Universities Students

Broadcasters in Ireland, Bulgaria, and Britain received threatening emails sent under the pseudonym “Mikhail Andropov,” while previous threats earlier in the week invoked a banned Russian extremist group. by Kyiv Post | Nov. 7, 2026, 3:18 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied An airplane of the KLM airline lands at the Vaclav Havel Airport in Prague, Czech Republic, Nov. 6. (Photo by Michal Cizek / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip A coordinated wave of false bomb threats targeted newsrooms and dozens of commercial passenger flights across several European nations on Friday, Nov. 6, prompting military fighter jet scrambles, flight diversions, and building evacuations, European authorities and news agencies reported. Accodring to Reuters , emailed threats titled “A Message to the West” and sent under the pseudonym “Mikhail Andropov” were delivered to Irish national broadcaster RTE, Bulgarian television network Nova TV, and British broadcaster Sky News. RTE temporarily evacuated staff from its Dublin headquarters before authorities cleared the facility. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Simultaneously, false bomb alerts targeted passenger airliners and airports across the Czech Republic, France , Denmark , and Italy . Advertisement In the Czech Republic , police reported threats directed at nine passenger aircraft at Prague Airport, leading to the diversion of one inbound flight to Venice, while Hungarian air force fighter jets and NATO combat aircraft escorted multiple passenger airliners through regional airspace. All reported threats were subsequently confirmed to be hoaxes. Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares characterized the coordinated wave of disruptions as an act of “hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare,” while the Irish government confirmed that the media alerts formed part of an organized cross-border campaign. Other Topics of Interest New Round of Ukraine Talks Set, European Representatives to Participate No date or venue has been announced for the next round of trilateral talks yet, although Witkoff confirmed it will include European partners. Who sent the threats and what were their demands? European security authorities are investigating whether the synchronized disruptions are connected to Western military and humanitarian support for Ukraine. The emails received by news outlets on Friday warned of catastrophic explosions unless European governments ceased assistance to Ukraine, though law enforcement agencies did not disclose specific operational details. The incidents follow similar bomb hoaxes distributed earlier in the week. On Thursday, Nov. 5, dozens of airports and commercial carriers received threats signed under the banner of “Male State,” an inactive Russian extremist organization banned in Russia . Advertisement A Telegram channel affiliated with the movement’s founder, Vladislav Pozdnyakov, denied responsibility for the campaign, claiming the group dissolved years ago and that unknown actors were exploiting the name to stage cross-border provocations. “Anyone currently orchestrating provocations within EU countries under the banner of this ‘brand’ is acting in their own self-interest – essentially flying someone else’s flag,” Pozdnyakov wrote on Telegram. Disruption to European aviation The Friday incidents mark the second major aviation disruption within 48 hours , following a wave of hoaxes on Thursday that disrupted at least 30 commercial passenger flights operated by Aer Lingus, Wizz Air, LOT Polish Airlines, Finnair, EasyJet, Iberia, and KLM. French fighter jets intercepted an Aer Lingus flight traveling from Dublin to Rome on Thursday, escorting the airliner to a military air base after the pilot reportedly refused an initial military directive, according to the office of French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. In Spain, national police reported receiving three separate emailed threats within 20 minutes targeting an Air Europa flight bound from Madrid to Paris alongside two inbound Iberia flights from Rome and Milan. Advertisement The Bulgarian Air Force escorted three commercial flights to emergency landings, while in Poland, an outbound LOT flight to Paris was halted on the tarmac in Warsaw, with passengers transferred to alternative aircraft. Italian airport authorities in Rome and Milan reported emails warning of explosive devices aboard flights arriving from Helsinki and Dublin. Aviation security analysts noted that while proving sovereign state attribution remains complex, the format aligns with asymmetric interference tactics. “When it comes to a situation like this or even other sabotage attacks, it’s really hard to prove there’s a certain country behind it. But it does fit in the modus operandi,” Eric Schouten, director of aviation security consultancy Dyami, told Reuters. European governments respond to hybrid threats The wave of bomb hoaxes unfolds amid persistent warnings from European intelligence agencies regarding an intensifying campaign of Russian hybrid operations across the continent. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski warned in late October that Russian hybrid warfare is expanding across the EU , pointing to arson attacks, attempted rail disruptions, and unauthorized drone activity near European critical transport nodes. Advertisement Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk similarly stated that Warsaw anticipates further escalations in hybrid threats before late December, following alerts from the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine (HUR) regarding covert sabotage plots aimed at European communications and military logistical infrastructure. In September, Denmark’s Defense Intelligence Service (DDIS) published a strategic assessment warning that hybrid threats encompass not only cyberattacks and physical sabotage against energy systems , but also deniable provocations designed to strain civil infrastructure and transport corridors supporting Ukraine.
